newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany still steadfastly opposed to IMF gold sale.
newsitem.headline: Germany still steadfastly opposed to IMF gold sale.

text.p: Germany is keen to resolve the financial problems of the world's poorest nations, but remains adamant that sales of International Monetary Fund gold are not the right way to fund debt relief, Bonn said on Wednesday.
German Finance minister Theo Waigel said in a statement released ahead of the meeting, "The federal government continues to reject a sale of IMF gold."

A senior official told a briefing in Bonn in advance of international meetings to be held in Washington later this week that Germany remained convinced that there were favourable alternatives to halp provide debt relief to the poor.
"We do not need to activate the IMF's gold resources to resolve the problems of a very limited number of countries," the official said.
Germany and a small number of other countries have joined forces to block a plan to sell a small amount of IMF gold to fund additional aid to a group of up to 20 very poor nations.
Their action, motivated by concern that such sales could set a bad precedent, has caused some irritation to other leading industrial countries, particularly the United States.
The U.S., along with other supporters of the gold sale plan, sees the proposal as a tidy way of providing relief to poor countries without tapping domestic budgets.

But the Bonn source said that the whole discussion about gold sales -- which he said had been proposed to stop a relatively small funding gap of about 1.1 billion dollars -- had been blown out of proportion.

"This whole argument is really about a completely different issue," the official said. "It has become a sort of status symbol whether the sales take place or not. But the decisive thing is to agree an initiative to help the poorest countries."
Germany is proposing direct debt forgiveness for poor countries from their creditors as a means to make sure the nations concerned do not collapse under their debt burdens.

The senior source said that Germany was prepared to raise the level of debt forgiveness offered to such weak nations to 80 percent, compared with the current maximum of 67 percent, providing a decision was made on a case-by-case basis and the other conditions attached to the deal were appropriate.

"Germany is prepared to agree that the debt forgiveness level of 67 percent could be raised to 80 percent in the cases of individual countries and if all other conditions are in place," the source said.

He made clear that Bonn would not agree to the 90 percent forgiveness level sought by the IMF and said that even this level was unacceptable to some countries in the Group of Seven rich nations, which will meet in Washington next week.
"Only 80 percent, not more," he said, adding "There is no consensus for 80 percent in the G7. At least one country has great problems with going above that."
But despite the diametrically opposed views on the gold sale plans, the source said he did not expect open conflict to break out in this month's Washington talks.

Referring to a row which broke out two years ago at a meeting in Madrid -- when rich and poor nations hit deadlock on a plan to issue more of the IMF's own currency, the Special Drawing Right -- the official said, "I assume one will want to avoid a situation like 1994."
Instead, the various committees were likely to confine their comments to welcoming the IMF's recently-announced decision to step up aid for the world's poorest nations.
The statement from IMF managing director Michel Camdessus this week pledged more aid for poor nations but neatly side-stepped the issue of how this would be offered.
